傑歌克主要見於巴厘島甘美蘭合奏，傳統中心在巴厘島西部，近年也在中部為遊客演出。它: The jegog is found mainly in Balinese gamelan ensembles, its traditional centre in western Bali, and in recent years groups have also performed in the centre for tourists. It can accompany dance, joined by kendang drums, cymbals and a small gong. Internationally, besides recordings, the Japanese group Geinoh Yamashirogumi used it in the soundtrack of the film Akira and in the last piece of Ecophony Rinne.
傑歌克以竹製體鳴鍵構成，鍵一端剖開、半管去除，另一端保留作共鳴，以木或橡膠槌敲擊: The jegog consists of bamboo idiophone keys, each split open at one end with half the tube removed and the other end left closed as a resonator, struck with wooden or rubber mallets; the source does not state how the volume is controlled. The ensemble spans about five octaves, the lowest instrument reaching sixty hertz, and its four-tone scale comes close to a dominant seventh chord; some keys are tuned in pairs so that, struck together at the same pitch, they beat. The music is fast, loud and rhythmically precise; the melody is played by several bamboo-key instruments together, the higher ones often playing interlocking rhythm patterns. Compared with the smaller bamboo-key tingklik, the large jegog uses long bamboo tubes as keys and needs two people squatting on the instrument to strike in turn.
傑歌克是源自印尼巴厘島的竹製甘美蘭合奏形式，傳統中心在西部金布拉納。樂器以竹管製: The jegog is a bamboo gamelan ensemble form from Bali, Indonesia, its traditional centre in Jembrana in the west. The instruments have keys made of bamboo tubes, split open at one end with the other end left closed as a resonator, hung on a wooden frame and struck with wooden or rubber mallets. The lowest instrument of the same name can be three metres long and needs two people squatting on it to play in turn; the ensemble contains melody instruments and instruments playing interlocking patterns, and it can also accompany dance, joined by drums, cymbals and a small gong. In recent years groups elsewhere in Bali have performed it for tourists.
傑歌克樂器以竹製發聲體為主，琴鍵多取竹管，一端剖開並去除半截管壁，另一端保留作共: The jegog instruments are mainly bamboo idiophones: the keys are mostly bamboo tubes, split open at one end with half the wall removed and the other end left closed as a resonator. The bamboo keys hang on a wooden frame and are struck with wooden or rubber mallets. There is also a smaller jegog tingklik, whose keys are bamboo strips set above a resonator box. Apart from bamboo, wood and the material of the mallets, the source does not state the materials of the other parts.
傑歌克起源於印尼巴厘島，是本土甘美蘭音樂形式，傳統中心在西部詹布拉納。近年擴展至: The jegog originated in Bali, Indonesia, as a local gamelan form, its traditional centre in Jembrana in the west. In recent years it has spread to other parts of Bali, with groups appearing in the centre performing for tourists; interest from tourists and from recordings has drawn international attention, and there are a few ensembles in Japan, the United States and Germany. The smaller ensembles have a longer history; when accompanying dance, drums, cymbals and a small gong may be added.
初學者可先從較小的 jegog tingklik 練習，其竹片鍵置於共鳴箱上方，: A beginner can start with the smaller jegog tingklik, whose bamboo-strip keys sit above a resonator box and are struck with a wooden or rubber panggul. The large jegog, with its long keys and heavy mallets, needs two people squatting on the top platform, striking the keys in turn. The undir is also played squatting on the platform. In the ensemble the barangan often strikes out a fast melody in alternation, while the kancil and suir play interlocking kotekan patterns.
